repos.title: EDGAR: Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure
repos.paper_summary: EDGAR is a diffusion-based refinement framework that corrects artifacts in Gaussian head avatars and then distills the refined renderings back into the avatar. The method adapts the one-step SD-Turbo backbone with a Sapiens identity-feature fusion block, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router with six experts, and an expression loss on POSTER V2 features. It is trained on EDGAR-SET, a triplet dataset of degraded renderings, ground-truth frames, and reference images built from real NeRSemble captures (99 identities) and synthetic CAFCA avatars (1,500 identities), with about half of pairs filtered by LPIPS. The refined multi-view renders then supervise a single Gaussian avatar with L1 and SSIM losses, so the final avatar renders without EDGAR and without added Gaussians. Experiments on CAP4D, GaussianAvatars, and RGBAvatar compare against raw outputs and an SDEdit-style baseline, reporting perceptual and reconstruction gains, cross-view consistency, and tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions. Limitations: the training data covers only recoverable degradations, severe structural errors in unobserved regions remain, and mean temporal error (tWE) rose for GaussianAvatars.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Monocular Gaussian avatars show artifacts, so EDGAR refines degraded renderings with a diffusion prior and reference identity.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior refinement methods use SDEdit-style noising that can alter identity, while EDGAR adds reference features and paired supervision.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: EDGAR-SET pairs simulated degraded renderings with ground truth and reference images, and EDGAR injects Sapiens features into a one-step diffusion model.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Against raw inputs and SDEdit, EDGAR leads most self-reenactment metrics, and 15 participants preferred it.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: EDGAR's gains vary by pipeline and metric, and severe structural errors in unobserved regions can remain.

repos.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
repos.paper_summary: Drex is a family of four open decision models that return a probability over each question's options without autoregressive decoding. The largest, Drex Max, is a 27B dense multimodal model that reads answers from a readout head with one logit per option code, up to 255 options. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with consistency losses, reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), and vision tuning. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max scores 67.52 on the public suite versus 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0. On Decision Bench v4 it reaches 94.0% accuracy, not significantly different from GPT-6 Sol and 1.6 points below Claude Opus 5.5. In a controlled ablation, RLAF adds 2.0 Decision Index points, and the consistency terms lower the top-1 flip rate from 6.3% to 4.2%. Limitations: all Drex models trail frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge benchmarks such as HLE and GPQA. Max's expected calibration error is 8.4% on questions with 6 to 20 options, and 13% of decisions with six or more options change their top option under reordering.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models read answers as option probabilities without decoding, for option sets supplied at inference time.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related work
digest_headlines.headline: The Drex models sit between option scoring, pointer networks, and calibration work, and each uses a different backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Problem formulation
digest_headlines.headline: A decision request holds a state and typed questions, and the model returns a distribution over each question's supplied options.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Pointer architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Pointer models encode the context once and score each option with a dot product between query and option-end states, with no decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Drex Max: a dense multimodal decision model
digest_headlines.headline: Drex Max removes the causal mask in full-attention layers of a 27B backbone and reads answers from a readout head over option codes.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training combines supervised fine-tuning with consistency losses and reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback, with vision tuning for Max.

digest_headlines.heading: 7 Experimental setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are compared on Decision Index 0.4.1, Decision Bench v4 and other suites, using Wilson intervals and exact McNemar tests on paired questions.

digest_headlines.heading: 8 Results
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover accuracy, calibration, option order, images and training stages, compared against decision-specialized and frontier chat models.

digest_headlines.heading: 9 Deployment and inference optimization
digest_headlines.headline: Shared prefill, graph capture and kernel changes cut latency, and answer-changing optimizations are accepted only within an accuracy threshold.

digest_headlines.heading: 10 Discussion and limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits: gaps to frontier chat models on closed-book knowledge, over-confidence in Max, and untested causes of its gains.

digest_headlines.heading: 11 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Drex Max leads the public Decision Index at 67.52, and its gains over the pointer models are not isolated to one design choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, question types and metrics, pointer masks, Drex Max kernel timings, deployment setups and Decision Index scoring.

repos.title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks
repos.paper_summary: This paper tests whether frontier LLMs can audit clinical prediction networks, separating tool-free reading of raw weights from computing with a calculator. Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated subarachnoid haemorrhage cohorts, with planted relationships, null networks, or a subgroup with under-recorded deaths. GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts, with weights in the prompt, or with a calculator that exposed either the weights or only predictions. Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but was unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction it declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks. With the calculator, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 null runs, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs. Black-box and white-box access performed alike, and a scripted analysis matched the comparator models on the audit. Limitations: simulated networks with simple planted forms, one model family, and cells with one to three runs.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Whether frontier models audit small clinical networks from raw weights or from computation has practical consequences for access.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier work covered weight reading, automated interpretability agents and clinical model audits, each under different access conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Networks trained on simulated cohorts with planted relationships were given to five GPT models under instruction and access conditions, scored by pre-written rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: With tools, GPT-6 Astra recovered planted relationships in all 29 runs up to 38,401 weights, while tool-free reading failed beyond 3,457 weights.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Results come from small simulated networks and one model family, with internal pre-specification and an adaptive design.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: With a calculation tool, GPT-6 Astra audited networks of up to 38,401 weights accurately, on a par with well-designed scripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: All simulated networks, prompts, replies, logs and evaluation code are released in a GitHub repository.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The study used only simulated data and involved no human participants.

digest_headlines.heading: Use of AI
digest_headlines.headline: Claude Opus 5.5 assisted with code, analyses and drafting, and the authors checked the results.

digest_headlines.heading: Competing interests
digest_headlines.headline: The authors declare no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The work received no specific funding.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists pre-specification commits and deviations, the explicit system instruction text, and an example prompt.

repos.title: CMDiff: Left Atrial Scar Segmentation from 3D LGE MRI Using Conditional Mask Diffusion Model: A Feasibility Study
repos.paper_summary: CMDiff is a 3D conditional mask diffusion model for left atrial (LA) scar segmentation from LGE cardiac MRI. Instead of predicting noise, it predicts the clean binary mask directly, conditioned on the LGE image through a lightweight Dynamic Conditional Encoder (DCE) that feeds multi-scale features into a 3D sinusoidal UNet via FiLM-like modulation. Training combines an SNR-weighted MSE diffusion loss with timestep-weighted soft Dice and BCE. Evaluation uses five-fold cross-validation on the 60 scar-labelled LASCARQS subjects (48 train, 12 held out per fold) against a matched deterministic baseline. Clean-mask prediction gives a scar DSC of 0.47 ± 0.08 and noise prediction gives 0.0006 ± 0.0003. CMDiff scores HD95 12.89 ± 6.39 mm and ASD 1.91 ± 0.96 mm, while the deterministic baseline scores DSC 0.51 ± 0.08, HD95 10.86 ± 5.39 mm, and ASD 1.58 ± 1.03 mm. Scheduler benchmarks find 20 to 50 reverse steps give the best DSC, and longer sampling adds cost without accuracy gains. The main limitations are the single public dataset of 60 scar cases, the slower iterative inference, and the absence of anatomy pretraining or explicit LA-wall constraints.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Thin, sparse left atrial scar on late gadolinium enhancement MRI makes segmentation hard, so the study tests 3D mask diffusion against a deterministic baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: CMDiff denoises a binary scar mask conditioned on the LGE image and predicts the clean mask directly rather than noise.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use five-fold cross-validation on 60 scar-labelled LASCARQS subjects, with 48 training and 12 held-out cases per fold.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Clean-mask prediction gives scar DSC 0.4675 against 0.0006 for noise prediction, but CMDiff trails the deterministic baseline on scar.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Conditional diffusion is feasible but not a performance advance here; explicit anatomy is a more important current lever.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The study establishes that direct mask diffusion is technically feasible for LA scar but does not outperform the deterministic baseline.

repos.title: Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation in Pixels, Interaction and World Space
repos.paper_summary: FAH is a family of hand-pose models built on SAM 3D Body's hand branch. The method predicts corresponding 2D and 3D hand joints and surface points with a heatmap head, then fits MANO or MHR-Hand meshes in a separate stage. Optional heads estimate anatomical parts and contact without object geometry at inference, a causal refiner smooths video tracks, and a camera model places hands in world space. In a controlled comparison within one network, directly predicted 3D points gave better mesh accuracy than predicting MANO parameters. On HOT3D v1, FAH-L reaches 4.31 mm PA-MPJPE and 8.89 mm root error at 65 fps with mesh fitting on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, against 6.72 mm PA for WiLoR and 9.46 mm PA for HaMeR (4.6 fps). The smallest model, FAH-S, runs at 101 fps. The paper names camera estimation as the main source of world-space error, and states that contact without object geometry remains ambiguous, with most contact vertices hidden on 96% of HOT3D contact hands.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Rig-based hand estimators propagate articulation errors to 2D landmarks, so FAH predicts points and fits meshes separately.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work regresses mesh parameters or vertices, and some contact methods need object shape and pose.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: FAH distills SAM 3D Body's hand branch into ViT students and predicts dense 2D and 3D points with a heatmap head.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the egocentric benchmark, the default FAH model's aligned joint error is 4.31 mm, below WiLoR's 6.72 mm.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Camera estimation dominates world-space error, and contact remains ambiguous without object geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training sources, teacher and student settings, label conventions, and image credits.

repos.title: AffineGS: Unlocking Accurate Geometry in 3DGS via Spatially Varying Affine Rectification
repos.paper_summary: AffineGS is a depth-regularized 3D Gaussian Splatting method that replaces global scale-and-shift alignment of monocular depth with spatially varying scale and shift fields. On MuSHRoom and ScanNet++, a single global transform fits 58.9% and 58.6% of Depth-Anything-V2 disparity pixels at a 0.02 residual threshold; five local regions reach 92.7% and 91.8%. The method estimates a per-pixel scale from disparity and rendered-depth gradients, derives a shift, clamps both to the 5th–95th percentiles, and smooths them with an edge-aware guided filter. Three losses supervise 3DGS: disparity-gradient matching, a normal-aware gradient term using camera intrinsics, and an L1 depth term after a global least-squares re-alignment. Limitations: the filter uses a 550–650 pixel radius on MuSHRoom, some scenes needed manually scaled loss weights, and initialization uses 1M back-projected sensor-depth points, so the pipeline is not fully sensor-free. The excerpt omits the main comparison tables, so no benchmark gains are reported here.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Monocular depth priors show region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions, so global alignment breaks down for 3DGS geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior depth-guided 3DGS methods fit one global scale-and-shift, and other extensions alter Gaussian primitives instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Spatially varying scale and shift fields rectify monocular disparity, then drive normal-aware gradient and depth losses.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The method cuts MuSHRoom Abs Rel to 0.0551 / 0.0490, versus 0.3542 / 0.3669 for DN-Splatter (Monodepth).

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The method approaches sensor-supervised geometric fidelity without any physical depth input.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists distortion tables across models and thresholds, extra figures, per-scene results and limitations.

repos.title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces a benchmark for indirect prompt injection (IPI) in which the attack tampers with a decision that a benign task already requires, rather than redirecting the agent to a new task. Planted content counts as IPI when it tries to influence a decision its source is not authorized to determine. The benchmark has 90 validated cases across productivity, DevOps, and marketplace tool environments, with 1,343 single-primitive attacks and one compound attack per case. Each attack targets one of six beliefs in the agent's decision process: objective, action-selection rule, consequence model, action-space model, observation interpretation, or world state. Across five LLMs without a defense, mean attack success is 17.0%. Objective attacks reach 15.0%, while decision-rule (21.2%), action-space (19.0%), and world-state (18.6%) attacks are higher. Detection-and-removal (DRIFT-iso) lowers objective attacks to 2.4%, but observation and state attacks remain at 9.5% and 12.1%. A tool-policy defense (Progent) leaves overall attack success at 15.4%, since tampered calls use tools the task needs. Limitations: all runs use simulated environments, and cases were drafted with LLM assistance and reviewed by the authors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing injection benchmarks mostly test instructions that redirect agents, so tampering with in-progress decisions goes untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks and defenses mostly assume instruction-bearing attacks, and each defense family limits a different kind of influence.

digest_headlines.heading: Threat Model
digest_headlines.headline: The attacker plants content in a role-appropriate source and can tamper with a decision the task consults that source for.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: The benchmark has 90 retained cases with 1,343 single-primitive attacks across productivity, DevOps, and marketplace environments.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Without a defense, decision-rule, action, and state attacks succeed more often than objective attacks, across five models.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Defenses tested mainly on redirecting instructions leave task tampering partly uncovered, so screening should also check source authority.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists construction stages, 18 attack categories, environment tools, scoring and validation checks, models, and limitations.

repos.title: The Gating Mechanism of KV Cache Eviction
repos.paper_summary: IndexMem++ is a KV cache eviction method that trains a lightweight, query-independent gate to score each cached entry by redundancy, plus a recovery branch of parameter-free centroid tokens for evicted information. The gate acts as a per-key logit bias inside the softmax, so suppressed attention mass moves to the retained entries. A constant bias cancels in the softmax, so naive training with the language-modeling loss collapses to near-constant scores. On Qwen3-0.6B at RULER 8K, that arm reaches 4.33, against 70.01 for dense attention. The method instead fixes the total gate mass of evictable entries, distills the dense model's next-token distribution with reverse KL, and allocates per-head budgets online by retained attention mass. On Qwen3-8B at 75% compression, it reaches 90.14 on RULER 8K and 46.03 on LongBench, 3.72 and 1.36 points below full-cache inference. Limitations: the ablations use a 0.6B model trained for 100 steps. Training the backbone jointly with the gate lowered RULER scores (62.83 against 71.65 for full KV in the reverse-KL setting). The provided text ends mid-section, so the history-based scorer results and the centroid recovery numbers are not fully shown.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Eviction should drop entries recoverable from the rest of the cache; the paper proposes an in-softmax gate with a recovery branch.

digest_headlines.heading: Attention mass and the eviction gate
digest_headlines.headline: A gate placed inside the softmax redistributes evicted mass to retained entries, while outer gates only scale values.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Naive training collapses to constant scores; fixed-mass competition, protected entries and distillation avoid that collapse.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: At 75% compression IndexMem++ reaches 90.14 on RULER 8K with Qwen3-8B, the highest of the compared methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior learnable eviction gates use similar scorers, while recovery methods differ in whether the summary shares the softmax.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A gate trained on the model's own loss keeps everything; fixed-mass competition, dense-model distillation and softmax readout fix this.

digest_headlines.heading: Future work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work proposes on-policy distillation, since the gate is trained on dense prefixes but applied to compressed caches.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, gate placements, additive biases, and retention analyses on long agent and math reasoning traces.

repos.title: Binding Paraphrased Instructions to Encountered Objects in sLLM Agents under Partial Observability
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces ALFWorld-Para, a benchmark that paraphrases ALFWorld goal instructions while preserving the task, and BINDIntent, a training-free method that binds paraphrased object expressions to labels the agent has already observed. The benchmark has 226 seen-split instructions, 29 paraphrase types, and 6,554 paraphrased instructions. RL-finetuned sLLM agents and prompted LLMs show 21–52% relative drops in success rate (SR), mostly from object synonyms. A 7B agent identifies synonym referents with nearly 80% accuracy but takes the target object in only 20–56% of synonym cases, versus over 90% under original labels. BINDIntent scores observed labels by cosine distance in ConceptNet Numberbatch embeddings, estimates with a Weibull model whether unseen candidates might match better, and substitutes the label into the instruction once binding is likely. It adds 0.4 ms of CPU time per step and no LLM calls. On synonym paraphrases it improves RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5–49.1 percentage points (pp). GiGPO-7B's overall SR rises from 61.8% to 77.4%, above prompted Mistral-Small-3-24B at 63.8%. The method targets object synonyms only. The paper does not test action-axis paraphrases such as Question and Hint, and it does not modify the agent's exploration policy.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Paraphrased instructions lower success of reinforcement-learning-tuned small agents, and a training-free binding method partly recovers it.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior robustness studies focus on system-side perturbations, leaving paraphrased user instructions for RL-finetuned agents largely unexamined.

digest_headlines.heading: ALFWorld-Para
digest_headlines.headline: Paraphrased goals cut success 21–52% relative, and RL-finetuned small models lose their edge over larger prompted models.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Object synonyms drive most failures, and agents often fail to take objects they already observed under synonyms.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Method
digest_headlines.headline: BINDIntent binds paraphrased object expressions to observed labels by embedding distance and estimated persistence against unseen candidates.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: BINDIntent raises GiGPO-7B overall success to 77.4, surpassing prompted Mistral-Small-3-24B.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Paraphrase failures stem from referent binding under partial observability, not knowledge loss, so fine-tuning alone may not suffice.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The method targets synonym-driven binding failures, leaving action-axis paraphrases and the exploration policy unaddressed.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers benchmark generation, human equivalence checks, codebases, extra per-type results, and ScienceWorld-Para analyses.

repos.title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), built from the singular values of equivariant GNN representations at each degree l. For discrete point-group identification, the method counts singular values above a numerical threshold at each degree and matches the resulting rank sequence to rank templates set by fixed-subspace dimensions. For continuous analysis, a leakage score (LS) gives the fraction of spectral energy beyond the target fixed-subspace dimensions, and pLS is its negative log10. A parameter-free equivariant GNN built from radial bases and spherical harmonics lets SymFP run without training. The paper shows that LS cannot increase when moving to a subgroup. Under regularity conditions, rank equality at one parameter setting holds for almost every parameter choice. On a synthetic set covering all 32 crystallographic point groups, degrees 0 to 9 distinguish every group, with identification accuracy of 99.06–100% across HEGNN, TFN, MACE, Equiformer and the parameter-free model. Limitations: rank counts depend on a numerical tolerance, and template matching assumes the representations span the fixed subspaces, which the paper reports for most but not all tested cases.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper treats structural symmetry as two tasks, point-group identification and continuous analysis, and proposes spectral fingerprints from equivariant representations for both.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Singular-value spectra of equivariant representations define a fingerprint that matches point groups through rank templates and scores symmetry leakage.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The constraints come from representation algebra, so the framework may extend beyond point groups to space groups and chirality.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Methods define graph compatibility, stabilizers and O(3) representations, and the datasets used for each analysis.

digest_headlines.heading: Data availability
digest_headlines.headline: Synthetic point clouds, Protein Data Bank entries and OpenFF torsion scans are the data sources behind the reported analyses.

digest_headlines.heading: Code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The SymFP implementation, training code and evaluation scripts are released in a GitHub repository.

digest_headlines.heading: Competing interests
digest_headlines.headline: The authors declare no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists Extended Data figures and tables on GNN spectra, p97, haemagglutinin, GluK2 and E18 capsids.
